The present book is the result of a long, and somewhal uneven, gestation. 1 be-
gan my work on a study of Babylonian and Assyrian text commentaries in the
late nineteen-nineties as a two-year post-doctoral fellow of the research group
“Religion und Normativitit,” founded by Jan Assmann and Theo Sundermeier at
Heidelberg University. After several years devoted mostly to other research and
a move to Yale University, a Morse fellowship granted by Yale in 2005/06 en-
abled me to retum to my commentary notes and transform them into a coherent
manuscript, which I submitted as my Habilitation thesis to the “Philosophische
Fakultat” of Heidelberg University in 2007. Various commitments prevented me
for two years from further work on the manuscript, but a sabbatical in 2009/10
gave me a chance to revise and finally submit it for publication.

1, Introduction

In his influential book on “the origin and goal of history,” written shortly after
World War 2, the German philosopher Karl Jaspers claimed that the period from
800 (o 200 BCE played a particularly crucial role in the intellectwal history of
‘man (Jaspers 1949). Jaspers argued that in the centuries in question, dubbed by
him the “axial age,” thinking, for the first time in human history, became the
object of itself. Jaspers distinguished China, India, and the eastern Mediterra-
nean as the three regions where this dawn of consciousness took place, but de-
clared with regard to the last area that it was only with the Hebrew prophets and
the Greek philosophers that the axial revolution really began. The earlier em-
pires of the region represented a pre-axial state.

Up to this day, Jasper's concept of an axial age has retained much of its at-
traction. Yet critical discussion of the concept during the past decades by schol
ars from different fields has made it increasingly clear that the civilizations of
Egypt and Mesopotamia were not as unaffected by “axial thinking" as Jaspers
had claimed.’ The present work deals with a group of Mesopotamian texts that
display various features of the self-conscious reflection Jaspers characterized as
axial: Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries or, to be more precise, text com-
mentaries. These commentaries are preserved in cuneiform script on more than
860 clay tablets from different archaeological sites in what is today the republic
of Ira. The tablets date to the period from the eighth to the second century
BCE, an era that coincides exactly with Jaspers’s axial age.’ The commentaries
represent efforts of Babylonian and Assyrian scholars to explain the whole range
of Babylonian literary, religious, and scholarly works, from epics and rituals to
legal, medical and omen texts. Using a plethora of hermencutical techniques, the
commentaries provide unique insights into many aspects of how the Mesopota-
mian mind, in its numerous avatars, actually worked.

If we regard hermeneutics as a set of intellectual tools that are applied to ar-
rive at a better understanding of the world, it would be wrong to claim that the
Babylonian and Assyrian text commentaries of the first millennium BCE are the
carliest testimonies of “hermeneutical reasoning” in human history. Hermeneu-
ics, in this most general sense, can be detected in almost every expression of the
human spirit, and Mesopotamia, with its ancient lexical tradition that goes back
to the birth of writing in the fourth millennium BCE, and its passion for divina~
tory quests, has lefl us large numbers of documents from much older periods to
study it." But if we define hermeneutics more narrowly as pertaining to the in-
terpretation of written texts, then Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries can
truly be regarded as a “first.” Physically separate from the texts they interpret,
these commentaries represent the earliest known corpus of exegetical treatises

The significance of the Babylonian and Assyrian commentary tradition is
thus threefold. First, the commentaries provide information on myriad aspects of
Mesopotamian languages and civilization. It is thanks to a medical commentary
from Babylonia, for instance, that we know how to pronounce the name Gilgame’,
normally written with a particularly enigmatic sequence of signs.’ Second, they
make it possible for us to investigate not only the central texts of ancient Meso-
potamia, but also the meaning assigned to these texts by those who read and studied
them, a meaning social anthropologists designate with the term “manifest con-
tent” (Cryer 1994, 208). And finally, when approached from a comparative per-
spective, the commentaries from Mesopotamia emerge as the earliest testimonies to
the long and complex history of textual interpretation, an intellectual pursuit prac-
ticed all over the world. To one particularly prominent chapter in this history, the
exegetical tradition of rabbinic Judaism, they may even be related genetically.*

and 47 autographs of two Nineveh commentaries, one astrological, the other

Lime still so much in their infancy that Norris, unaware of what the texts actually
represented, characterized them simply as bilingual lists. Progress in the analysis,

1.2. Scope and limits of the present study

This book provides a new introduction to the text commentaries from Babylonia
and Assyria, It first describes the Mesopotamian philological and divinatory
traditions from which the commentaries emerged (ch. 2), then discusses their
temporal and geographic distribution (ch. 3), and in the following chapters deals
with their typology (ch. 4), hermeneutical techniques (ch. 5), and sources (ch. 6).
Chapter 7 is a catalogue of all available commentaries, organized according to
the texts which they explain. Chapter 8 provides information on the individuals
who copied and studied commentaries, and on the academic, political, and eso-
tcric dimensions of Mesopotamian exegesis, while chapter 9 investigates the
conditions that led to the emergence of the commentary tradition. The last sec-
tion of the book has a somewhat supplementary character. It includes a short
overview of explanatory texts and cultic commentaries (ch. 10), a case study of
how a particularly important text, the Babylonian Epic of Creation, was ex-
plained, re-interpreted, and rewritten over the centuries (ch. 11), and a brief
discussion of the legacy of Mesopotamian hermeneutics (ch, 12). An appendix
provides full editions of two commentary tablets, as well as statistical summa-
ries of some key issues.

2.1.2. Glosses

Giosses are notes writen by scribes into the texts copied by them. Inscribed
between the lines or on the left edge of the tablet, they can have different purposes.
Glosses writen in smaller script indicate the pronunciation of difficult logograms or
rarely used syllabic values, or they provide, as in the case of many Sumerian texts
copied by students during the Old Babylonian period,” Akkadian translations of
individual words and phrases. The gloss hepi ess “new break” indicates that the
tablet from which the scribe copied his text was damaged, while fiepi labiru “old
break” points to a note about stich a break in an earlier manuscript. Glosses can
also be marked, most commonly in the first millennium, by separating cola nor-
mally consisting of two diagonal wedges (“Glossenkeile”). Usually, glosses of
this type provide alternative readings that had to be noted when a scribe copied
from deviating versions of the same text. Outside of Mesopotamia, separating
cola would introduce translations of Akkadian terms into local languages, such
as Hurrian and Canaanite, or mark foreign words.

Mesopotamian civilization was, in many ways, multilingual, a fact that is re-

They dealt with the vast area of divine signs that were believed to be detectable, for those who possessed the necessary knowledge, on the exta of the sacrificial sheep, in the life of plants, the behavior of animals and humans, or in the movement of the heavenly bodies. Mesopotamian omen texts 23 There is little doubt that the enormous amount of thought that Mesopotamian scholars put into their divinatory tradition had a large impact on the rise of the Babylonian and Assyrian text commentary. In an intellectual environment conceptualized the world as a text in need of interpretation, it was not that great a step to turn to an interpretation of texts proper. The omen compendia them- selves were, incidentally, the first texts to be commented on, and they the most important genre dealt with by commentators until the end of cuneiform civilization. Originally created to explain extra-textual signs, their own intra- textual components — cuneiform characters, words, and sentences - required more and more explanation as time went by.

Early rabbinic scholarship has left us three lists of hermeneutic “rules” for how
to interpret the Hebrew Bible: the seven, thirteen, or thirty-two middot ascribed
to Hillel, Ishmael, and Eliezer ben Yose, respectively.” They represent differ-
cent approaches to an explicit “theory” of hermeneutics. The scholars of Babylo-
nia and Assyria did apparently not produce such a theory ~ at least, they never
put it into writing. This leaves the task of identifying the basic principles and
procedures of cuneiform hermeneutics to the modem scholar, who has to deduce
them by means of studying individual commentary entries.”

Beginning with the fairly simple and moving towards the more complicated,
this chapter will provide an overview and examples of the most important com-
mentarial techniques used by Mesopotamian exegetes.””” The fundamental dis-
tinction between literal and non-literal modes of interpretation, for which the
ancient scholars had their own terminology, has been discussed in 4.2 and is not
a factor in the more detailed classification of hermeneutical procedures provided
here, Yet it will come as no surprise that to give simple synonyms normally
leads to a literal interpretation of a passage, while etymological and etymographical
analysis yields itself more to an “allegorical” approach. Some of the herme-
neutical techniques described below are primarily geared towards bridging the
gap between the cultural horizons of the ancient text and the commentator (see,
especially, 5.1.1 and 5.1.5), while others provide supplementary knowledge on
cuneiform signs or various linguistic phenomena (5.1.4, 5.1.6).

The number of examples given on the following pages is kept fairly small.
More examples can be found in ch. 6, which discusses quotations from other
texts constituting or accompanying commentarial explanations, ch. 7, which
presents an overview, with their base texts, of all known commentaries from

Etymology and etymography It has already been pointed out, in 4.4, that Babylonian and Assyrian scholars analyzed not only the content of a text, but also its expressive substance, that is, the sound of its words and the signs with which these words are written. Com- mentaries, to phrase it differently, do not only provide synonyms but also homo- nyms (or close homonyms) — words that sound exactly like or similar to a given Jemma even though they may mean something completely different; and they analyze the signs used to write individual lemmata with an eye on the many other meanings these signs may have. Both which we can call ety- mological and etymographical, were instrumental for the com- mentators to arrive at non-literal interpretations of a given text. Etymology and etymography were particularly important for the explanation of larger text units, as will be shown in 5.2, but the techniques were also used to deal with individual words and short phrases. These be- liefs provide the foundation for their strategy to interpret individual elements of Akkadian words (as well as names and logograms) in the light of Sumerian. The technique they used to isolate small word components suitable for such analysis is reminiscent of what is known from later rabbinical tradition as notarikon. A good example of its application is an entry in K 778. a commentary on EAE 15.“ Obv. 3-4 this tablet deal with the Akkadian word bardri (written ba-ra- ri) “at dusk,” which, in the omen commented on, specifies the time of the occur- rence of lunar eclipse. 6. Sources of the explanations particularly striking feature of the cuneiform exegetical tradition is its ano- nymity. Subscripts on commentary tablets, while declaring that at least some of their explanations go back to certain “(master-)scholars” (Sa pi umméni), never actually identify these scholars by name.*”* Such anonymity suggests that in Mesopotamia, unlike later rabbinical, Greco-Roman, Islamic, and Chris- tian traditions, it was apparently not only, and perhaps even not primarily, the commentator who provided the commentary with authority. Yet the ies, were frequently copied, evidently did possess authority, and so the question arises where this authority actually came from. One answer seems to be that it derived from various canonical texts — texts that were excerpted and reproduced in the very explanations put forward in the commentaries. For many of these explanations are clearly not just some exe- gete’s ad hoc attempts at understanding. They are, instead, quotations taken textual record that constituted the Mesopotamian “stream of tradi- tion." Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries are not only meta-texts, that is, texts that say something new about other texts, but also juxtapose passages from two or more different “pre-texts."“7* the modem student of Mesopotamian hermeneutics faces a serious problem: Only rarely do commentaries offer explicit references to the sources of their explanations. The only texts quoted in commentaries from eighth and seventh century Assyria are lexical lists and explanatory texts, while the later Babylonian commentaries also provide quotations, many of them fairly long, from magico-medical, reli- gious, legal, and literary texts. At first glance, one might be inclined to attribute this difference to an opposition between Assyrian and Babylonian hermeneutics, but this is not a very likely solution since many of the commentaries from As- syria seem to draw on Babylonian traditions. 7.1.1. Eniima elis

Also called the “Babylonian epic of creation,” Eniima eli describes in seven tablets
how the world came into being and how the god Marduk of Babylon became its
ruler after defeating the ancient matriarch Tiamat, a dragon-like creature represent-
ing the sca, who was accompanied by a host of terrifying monsters. One of the
text’s most important functions was to provide an etiology of the religious and
political predominance claimed by the city of Babylon. The text's date of com-
Position is much disputed, with suggestions ranging from the reign of Hammurapi to
the early first millennium. Some indications point towards the time of Nebuchad-
nezzar T (1125-1104 BCE) as the period when the epic was most likely written,
Eniima eli was recited on the occasion of important religious festivals, notably the
Akitu festival celebrated in Babylon at the beginning of the year, and intensively
studied in elementary education in first millennium Babylonia.>” Its reception in
Assyria, Babylonia, and beyond will be discussed at greater length in ch. 11.5”

Eniima elis is accessible in numerous translations, among them recent ones
in English by Foster (2005, 436-86) and Lambert (2008, 35-59). No up-to-date
scholarly edition of it is at present available, but a new “pedagogical” edition
has recently been provided by Talon (2005); it should be consulted together with
the important reviews by Borger (2008) and Oelsner (2009).

Commentaries on Eniima elis are known since the beginning of the last cen-
tury, when King published some pertinent fragments (1902, 157-175). They can
be divided into several groups: a commentary that covers the whole epic, three
manuscripts of a commentary on tablet VII, some exegetical texts that deal with
Eniima elig but are not text commentaries stricto sensu, and some unpublished
tablets whose commentarial relationship to the epic remains to be established,

Ludlul bél némeqi Ludlul, also called “The Poem of the Righteous Sufferer” because of its similari- ties with the Biblical book of Job, is a poetic monologue in four tablets in which a Babylonian nobleman, once rich and powerful, describes how he was forsaken by the god Marduk and suffered all kinds of hardship before finally being saved by the god and restored to his former position. The text, edited by Lambert, BWL, 21-62, 283-302, newly translated by Foster (2005, 392-409), and recently re-edited, with new manuscripts, by Annus & Lenzi (2010), draws on a wide- ranging vocabulary with numerous Aapax legomena, making it a typical exam- ple of the highly learned style that characterizes Babylonian literature of the Kassite and Isin II periods. It was probably composed at some point during the period between the reign of NazimaruttaS (1307-1282 BCE) and the eleventh century BCE. Ludlul must have been difficult to understand for the Assyrian and Babylo- nian scholars who studied the text in the first millennium, and it therefore comes as no surprise to find that a rather long one-column commentary from Nineveh, K 3291 (C: BWL, pl. 15-17, E: ibid., 31-56), seeks to elucidate it. The main purpose of this commentary is to clarify rare words; farru (III 40), for instance, which literally means “bearded,” is explained as dannu “strong” (rev. 7). The commentary is structured in such a way that it quotes a line from Ludlul, repeats the lemma that requires explanation (usually in the form of an infinitive or nominative), and then provides an Akkadian synonym for it. The “Babylonian Theodicy” Like Ludlul, the “Babylonian Theodicy,” another Babylonian wisdom text (BWL, 63-91, translation: Foster 2005, 914-22), struggles with the problem of divine justice. The “Theodicy” is a dialogue between a sufferer and his who confront each other in stanzas of eleven lines each, all beginning with the same syllable. extant portions of “Marduk’s Address,” some only known from commentaries,

other deities to expel the evil spirits.

7.3.1, Astrology (Eniima Anu Enlil)

Even though astrology was already practiced in the third millennium, the earliest
collections of astrological omens, most of them on lunar phenomena, date only
to the Old Babylonian period No generally accepted series was yet established by
that time, and no such series is attested for much of the second half of the second
millennium, which bas yielded a vast array of rather diverse astrological texts, both
from Mesopotamia and the periphery (Susa, Emar, Qatna, Alalah, Ugarit, and
‘attuga), It must have been towards the end of the second millennium that many of
these texts were finally put together, in modified versions, to create what would
become the “canonical” series on astrology in the first millennium: Eniima Anu Enlil
(henceforth: EAE). This text, known from thousands of manuscripts from all
major scribal centers of Mesopotamia, but most prominently from Nineveh and
Babylon, was regarded by later tradition as the work of Ea, the god of wisdom.“
Both EAE catalogues and subscripts on actual EAE manuscripts demonstrate
that the distribution of the text on individual tablets was not completely fixed in
the first millennium. We know that one version of EAE consisted of seventy
tablets, while other versions were inscribed on fewer tablets.“* The sequence
and the phrasing of omens could differ as well. Such variation testifies to a
rather high amount of instability in the textual tradition, yet one must at the
same time acknowledge that the various recensions of EAE all share the same
basic structure. First, a section called tdmaratu Sa Sin “sightings of (the moon
god) Sin” describes different lunar phenomena (EAE 1-14 in the tradition repre-
sented by the Assyrian Nineveh texts). Then follow sections on lunar eclipses
(EAE 15-22(23)), various solar phenomena (EAE 23(24)-29(30)), solar eclipses
(30(31)-35(36)), meteorological phenomena (clouds, winds, thunder, lightning,
and, somewhat surprisingly, earthquakes) (EAE 36(37)-49(50)), and, finally,
planetary and astral observations (EAE 50(51)-70)."" The four main parts of

Unlike astrology, extispicy was a divinatory procedure that aimed at verifica- tion, not at prognostication (Pongratz-Leisten 1999, 128). It answered a specific question asked by someone. The only issue of importance was whether the apodosis was auspicious or inauspicious — and it is therefore not surprising that most commentaries on extispicy omens focus on the protases of the relevant texts, Until the first millennium, when its prestige began to be matched, and was eventually surpassed, by that of extispicy had been Mesopotamia’s most esteemed discipline of divination.” Attempts by later tradition to Tetroject its beginnings to the reign of the antediluvian king Enmeduranki of Sippar are obviously unrcliable (Lambert 1998), but there is no question that the practice of making decisions based on an inspection of the internal organs of a sacrificial animal was indeed very old; it is attested in contemporary sources from the 26!" century onwards. Physiognomic omens (Alamdimmi) Babylonian and Assyrian scholars believed that physiognomy, the observation 1 of physical features of a healthy man or woman, and an analysis of his or her behavior, would yield important clues for establishing the future destiny of that person.” From the Old Babylonian period onwards, they collected pertinent observations in large omen compendia, many of which were eventually united in a “canonical” series compiled by Esagil-kin-apli, an eleventh century scholar who also created the diagnostic compendium Sa-gig (sce 7.4.1). Esagil-kin-apli’s physiognomic omen series, called Alamdimmi “physique, form,” is attested in first millennium copies from Nineveh, Assur, Kalhu, Baby- lon, Sippar, and Uruk. It comprises five sections, or chapters, the first of which; Alamdimmi, gave the whole work its name. This first chapter, the largest and most important of the series, consists of twelve tablets with various | physical features observed on the body of a man. The series’s other chapters are... © { Nigdimdimmi, on the behavior of men (2), Kataduggit, on verbal utterances and what they signify (3), Summa sinnistu gaqgadu rabét, on physical features of as women (4), and Summa liptu, on moles and similar body marks (5). Medical texts 219 Mesopotamia by John Wee is in an advanced stage of preparation. 7.4.1. and texts Medicine was practiced in Mesopotamia from earliest times onwards, but it was only during the Old Babylonian period that Babylonian healers started to com- pose written compendia with systematic descriptions of individual symptoms observed on the body of a sick !0! Its findspot is known to have produced many Anu-iksur tablets. 7.4.2. texts Therapeutic medicine was a time-honored discipline in ancient Mesopotamia. Written sources dealing with physicians and medical procedures, among them administrative documents, letters, law codes, and literary texts, are attested from the third millennium No other texts, however, tell us more about the healing strategies Babylonian and Assyrian physicians applied than the nu- merous cuneiform compendia that provide directions on the treatment and care of patients. Dealing with a vast array of diseases, their entries typically comprise three sections: a description, frequently introduced by Summa “if,” of the symp- toms from which the patient suffered, prescriptions for the preparation of drugs and other substances to fight the affliction, and orders on how to apply them. Medication was administered in the form of potions, fumigations, ointments, or More devices such as semi-precious stones put on necklaces played a role as and often, incantations and prayers would accompany the treatment. Babylonian and Assyrian therapeutic texts represent a more complex and less well-explored genre than the diagnostic and prognostic tradition. Subscripts on tablets from first millennium Nineveh and Uruk indicate that efforts were made by the scribes of later periods to serialize the therapeutic corpus. Assurbanipal’s libraries have produced several therapeutic mini-series that include between two and six tablets, among them, for example, Summa amilu sudlu marus “If a man suffers from (BAM 574-79, five tablets) and Summa amilu indiu marsd “If a man’s eyes are afflicted” (BAM 510-16, three tablets). At some point, these mini-series were combined into a large series that was named, after its first chapter, Summa amilu mubhasu ummu ukdl “If the top of a man’s head is intensely hot.” It was apparently organized according to the principle a capite ad calcem. The text was written on large monuments, among them the famous stela from Susa now housed in the Louvre, which is our most valuable source for the text. But it also became one of the central cultural texts of the Mesopotamian “stream of tradi- tion.” While there is little evidence that Hammurapi’s law collection was ever strictly applied in the courts, its importance as a text that was studied in school and handed down from generation to generation of scholars is well documented. The laws provided a lasting model of ideal justice, and the language they were cast in continued to be held in the highest regard. Copies of the laws from both Babylo- nia and Assyria abound, with the last ones dating to the Late Babylonian period. The Laws of Hammurapi are divided into three parts: a prologue outlining Hammurapi’s divine election as a lawgiver, the main section of the text with its almost 300 laws, and an epilogue demanding respect for the laws and inviting those subjected to wrongdoing to consult them. Useful editions of the text are Borger 1979, 2-50 and Roth 1995, 71-142. 8. The socio-cultural milieu of Mesopotamian commentary
studies

Assyriology, in many ways a field confronted by significant obstacles ~ lexical
and grammatical uncertainties, broken texts, a tradition lost for almost 2000
years — has one significant advantage over a discipline like classics: the original
setting of its literary and scholarly texts is, in many cases, well known. A large
number of Assyrian and Babylonian clay tablets were discovered in the build-
ings where they were studied and stored in antiquity," and many have colo-
phons that provide information on their owners and scribes, the whereabouts of
the originals from which they were copied, the dates of these copies, and the
reasons for producing them. Thanks to such colophons, we can often assess the
socio-cultural context even of tablets that originate from undocumented excava-
tions or secondary locations.

Drawing on the information provided by colophons and archaeological con-
text, this chapter will present a short overview of the Assyrian and Babylonian
scriptoria and libraries where commentaries were studied and housed, of the
‘owners of commentary tablets, and of the students and scribes who copied them.
Of course, remarks on the social background of these individuals will have to be
concise, and only limited information can be given on their broader intellectual
interests as mirrored by other tablets written and owned by them. Bibliographi-
cal references will have to be selective as well.'"”

Questions regarding the origins of the commentary tradition and its indebt-
edness to processes of canonization and textualization will not be treated here;
they will instead be dealt with in ch. 9.

8.3.4. Babylon and Borsippa

Babylon, ancient metropolis, capital of the Chaldaean empire, and last strong-
hold of Babylonian traditions, may have been, together with its sister city Bor-
sippa, the most important center of cuneiform learning in first millennium
Mesopotamia. Due to the chances of discovery, scholarly tablets from Babylon
dating to the early centuries of the first millennium are rare, but large numbers
of such tablets have been found that were written between ca, 600 BCE and the
beginning of the Common Era. They testify to Babylon’s continuing status as an
intellectual hub during the centuries of slow decline that Mesopotamian civiliza-
tion experienced after the loss of political independence in 39 BCE. Regretta-
bly, most of these tablets come from excavations in the eightcen-seventies and
early eighteen-cighties that were very poorly documented. The later, far better
documented archacological investigations undertaken between 1899 and 1917
by Robert Koldewey on behalf of the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft yielded
much smaller numbers of scholarly texts.'“** Yet thanks to recent contributions
by Reade (CBT VI, xii-xxxviii), van Driel (1989), and especially Clancier
(2005b, 193-335, 2009, 105-213, 409-70), it is nonetheless possible to venture
some hypotheses regarding the original setting of the tablets uncarthed by the
carlier excavations.

8.4. The cultural setting of Mesopotamian hermeneutics 315

To what extent established scholars of the first millennium valued commen-
taries and regarded them as intellectual resources to be drawn on can be inferred
from a number of additional observations. Many commentary tablets have catch-
lines, indicating that commentaries were organized in large series. Some end with
prayers,'” while others include curses against those who might steal them. It was
acceptable to borrow commentary tablets, but only under the provision that the
borrower handed them back within the lending period.'™ Occasionally, com-
mentaries travelled from one city to another. Assurbanipal’s army of scribes and
the Assyrian “intellectual” Nabi-zuqup-kénu copied commentary tablets that had
been brought to Assyria from Babylon and Borsippa, and the Uruk scholar IgiSaya
kept in his private library commentary tablets from Nineveh and Nippur, some of
which may later have found a new home in the Bit réS temple. All this confirms
the impression that commentary tablets were much more than mere teaching tools.
But why were commentaries such valued possessions? What additional fune-
tions did they perform? Two particularly important and fundamental functions seem
to stand out. First, there is the pragmatic dimension of the commentary tradition:
commentaries were referred to by leamed professionals to find answers to specific
inquiries. For example, exegetical treatises on divinatory texts helped Nineveh
scholars who reported ominous signs to the Assyrian king to interpret these signs
in ways that were in harmony with the political exigencies of the time (see 8.2.4.4).
Commentaries on medical texts would give physicians additional information on
the symptoms of specific diseases or the nature of certain plants, thereby facilitating
the diagnosis and treatment of an ailment described all too briefly in the base
text. And the fact that commentaries from the “house of the exorcists” in Assur
include passages culled from different magical series may imply that the ritual
segments commented on were selected with an eye on the sequence in which
they occurred in the magical rites the exorcists actually performed (sce 8.2.2.1).
‘Commentaries, however, could also have a second, more philosophical goal:
to demonstrate the consistency and multi-layered wisdom of the texts they ex-
plained. This is what the commentary on the names of Marduk listed in Eniima
eli§ VII (7.1.1.2) tries to achieve, an elaborate exercise in etymologically in-

apodoses, and to demonstrate that the drugs and other substances employed by

338 9. Canonization and the formation of the commentary tradition

Earlier, in 8.4, 1 have highlighted some of the factors that were instrumental
for the flourishing of commentarial studies in first millennium Mesopotamia: the
commentaries’ usefulness in education, their pragmatic qualities in the fields of
divination and medicine, and their potential to satisfy a growing need for “mys-
tical” speculation. But the most important incentive for Assyrians and Babylo-
nian scholars to compose and study commentaries was perhaps the need to keep
the canonical compositions that had been ereated at the end of the second mil-
Jennium somehow accessible to later generations. These compositions, in which
the “stream of tradition” had been frozen, became more and more obscure in the
rapidly changing culture of first millennium Mesopotamia, and the linguistic
transformations that took place during this period, especially the slow decline of
Akkadian and the rise of Aramaic, presented an ever growing challenge to their
proper understanding. Since translation into Aramaic was apparently not re-

11. A case study of Mesopotamian hermeneutics: The
reception history of Eniima elig'””

The focus the present study places on text commentaries might give the impres-
sion that commentaries were the only vehicle for first millennium Mesopota-
mian scholars to deal with culturally significant texts. Yet such a view would be
mistaken, There were also other means by which (0 respond to the challenges
posed by such works. One was to produce new texts that reacted to earlier
ones,!" in some cases (in which we can speak of “counter-texts”) completely
reversing their plots. Small but significant manipulations of older works were
another way to adapt texts to the needs of a later era and to produce new mean-
ings, even though the canonical status many written compositions had acquired
in the late period put limits to this form of textual accommodation. Finally, texts
that had been forced on a community by powerful political elites that sought to
disseminate their ideologies could be simply repressed once the community had
been freed from the influences that had imposed these texts.

elis). The chapter includes observations on the cultic and theological contexts of
the epic, and how they became the subject of interpretation as well.’
